stories.title: Why drinking water matters
stories.summary: Water does a lot of quiet work in your body. A quick look at why it's worth the habit.

body.text: Water makes up more than half of your body. It carries nutrients to your cells, helps control your temperature, cushions your joints and lets your kidneys clear waste.
What steady drinking helps with

items: Clearer thinking and fewer afternoon slumps
Fewer headaches caused by not drinking enough
Healthy kidneys and regular digestion
Staying cool in hot weather and during exercise

body.text: Small, regular drinks through the day work better than a lot at once. That's what your reminders are for.
More stories arrive here over time, with tips for meals, sleep and staying on track.

source.label: NHS: Water, drinks and your health

stories.title: Steady water, happy kidneys
stories.summary: Your kidneys filter your blood all day. Here's how regular sips help them do it.

body.text: Your kidneys filter your blood around the clock, removing waste and extra salt in your urine. To do that well, they need enough water to work with.
Why steady beats a lot at once
Drinking regularly through the day keeps your urine diluted. Dilute urine makes it harder for minerals to clump together, which is one of the ways kidney stones form.

items: Pale yellow urine is a good sign you're drinking enough.
Dark yellow urine usually means you need more.
Hot weather, exercise and illness raise how much you need.

body.text: Spread your drinks out: a glass with each meal and a few in between is easier on your body than a big amount in one go.
If you have a kidney or heart condition, your doctor may give you a different amount to drink. Follow their advice.

stories.title: How much water do you need a day?
stories.summary: 6 to 8 glasses is a good start. Here's what makes you need more, and how to tell you're getting enough.

body.text: A common guide for adults is 6 to 8 glasses of fluid a day, about 1.5 to 2 litres. It's a starting point, not a strict rule: some days you'll need more.
What makes you need more

items: Hot or humid weather
Exercise or a physical job
Being ill, especially with a fever, sickness or diarrhoea
Pregnancy and breastfeeding

body.text: Food counts too. Fruit, vegetables, soups and yoghurt all add some water to your day.
How to tell you're getting enough
Pale yellow pee is a good sign. Dark yellow pee, peeing less often or feeling thirsty a lot usually means you need to drink more.
Don't try to drink it all at once. A glass with each meal and one or two in between gets you most of the way, and your reminders can do the counting.

stories.title: Start the day with a glass
stories.summary: You wake up after hours without a drink. One glass is an easy first win.

body.text: While you sleep you still lose water through your breath and skin, and you don't drink for seven or eight hours. Many people wake up a little behind.
Make it automatic

items: Leave a full glass or bottle next to your bed.
Drink it before your phone, coffee or tea.
Log it right away, so your day starts with progress.

body.text: Tying a new habit to something you already do every morning, like brushing your teeth, makes it much easier to keep.

source.label: NHS: Water, drinks and your health

stories.title: Water with breakfast
stories.summary: A glass with your first meal tops up what the night took and sets your pace.

body.text: Breakfast is a natural moment to drink. A glass of water alongside it helps you catch up after the night, and it's an easy habit to repeat every day.
How much?
A regular glass (around 250 ml) is plenty. Tea, coffee and milk count toward your daily total too, though plain water is the simplest choice.
If you're rushing in the morning, drink your glass while breakfast cooks or the kettle boils.

source.label: NHS: Water, drinks and your health

stories.title: Around lunch: before, during, after
stories.summary: Afternoon slumps are often a little thirst. Here's an easy rhythm for midday.

body.text: Midday is when many people fall behind: busy mornings, meetings, errands. Lunch is a good moment to catch up.
An easy midday rhythm

items: A glass before you eat can help you notice when you're full.
Sip during the meal; drinking with food is fine for most people.
Have another glass in the hour after lunch, when tiredness tends to set in.

body.text: Feeling sleepy or unfocused in the afternoon? Try a glass of water before reaching for a snack or another coffee.

stories.title: After dinner and before bed
stories.summary: Finish the day well without waking up at night to use the toilet.

body.text: A glass with dinner helps you reach your goal. In the last hour or two before bed, small sips are better than big glasses.
Sleep well and stay on track

items: Drink most of your water before the evening.
Have a glass with dinner.
Keep only a few sips for the last hour before sleep.

body.text: If you often wake up at night to use the toilet, move more of your drinking earlier in the day.

source.label: NHS: Water, drinks and your health

stories.title: Do tea, coffee and milk count?
stories.summary: Water is best, but it isn't the only drink that counts. Here's what does, and what to keep small.

body.text: Water is the best everyday drink, but it isn't the only one. Lower-fat milk and lower-sugar drinks, including tea and coffee, all count towards your daily fluid.
Tea and coffee
They count, but keep caffeine moderate. Some people are more sensitive to it than others, so notice how it affects your sleep and how you feel.
Drinks to keep small

items: Fruit juice and smoothies: one small glass (150 ml) a day, with a meal, because they're high in sugar.
Fizzy and sugary drinks: swap them for water or sugar-free versions.
Squash and cordials: dilute them well.

body.text: Make plain water more tempting: add a slice of lemon or cucumber, or a few mint leaves.

stories.title: Foods that help you stay hydrated
stories.summary: Some of your water comes from your plate. These foods are full of it.

body.text: Not all of your water comes from drinks. Many fruits and vegetables are mostly water, and they bring vitamins, minerals and fibre too.
Water-rich choices

items: Cucumber, lettuce and tomatoes
Watermelon and other melons
Oranges and strawberries
Soups, stews and yoghurt

body.text: Add one water-rich fruit or vegetable to each meal. It counts towards your 5 a day as well.
Food helps, but it doesn't replace drinking. Keep sipping through the day too.

stories.title: Drinking water when you exercise
stories.summary: Sweat is mostly water. A little planning before, during and after keeps you going.

body.text: When you move, you sweat, and sweat is mostly water. Lose too much and exercise feels harder, and you may feel tired or light-headed afterwards.
Before, during and after

items: Before: have a drink in the hour or two before you start.
During: take small sips, especially in long or hot sessions.
After: keep drinking little and often for a while to replace what you lost.

body.text: Take a bottle with you to the gym, on a walk or on a run, so you don't have to wait until you're home.
For everyday exercise, plain water is all most people need.

stories.title: Staying hydrated in hot weather
stories.summary: In the heat you lose more water than you think. Simple ways to keep up and stay cool.

body.text: In hot weather you sweat more, so your body needs more fluid than usual, even on days when you're not very active.
Simple ways to keep cool

items: Drink extra fluids, and don't wait until you're thirsty.
Have cold drinks and cool food; go easy on alcohol, caffeine and hot drinks.
Carry water when you go out.
Stay out of the sun at the hottest time of the day.

body.text: Check on older relatives, babies and young children in a heatwave: they're more at risk.
If you feel dizzy, confused or very weak in the heat, move somewhere cool, drink water and get medical help if it doesn't pass.

source.label: NHS: Heatwave: how to cope in hot weather

stories.title: Tired or headachy? Try water first
stories.summary: Not drinking enough is a common cause of headaches and tiredness, and one of the easiest to fix.

body.text: Not drinking enough fluid is one of the common causes of headaches. Being low on water can also leave you feeling tired, light-headed or dizzy.
When it might be water

items: A headache that creeps in during a busy day
Feeling tired or sluggish in the afternoon
A dry mouth and dark yellow pee

body.text: Keep a glass or bottle on your desk. Seeing it is the easiest reminder to sip.
Headaches have many causes. If one is very bad, keeps coming back or doesn't get better, talk to a doctor or pharmacist.

stories.title: Signs you need more water
stories.summary: Thirst isn't the only signal. Learn the early signs so you can act sooner.

body.text: By the time you feel very thirsty, your body has been asking for water for a while. These early signs are worth noticing.

items: Dark yellow, strong-smelling urine
Feeling tired or dizzy
A dry mouth, lips or eyes
Headaches
Peeing only a little, fewer than 4 times a day

body.text: Most of the time, a few glasses of water over the next hours is enough. If signs are severe or don't improve, contact a doctor.
